title: What's the bar exam like anyway?
summary: Josh and Chuck (iHeart Intro) explore the bar exam: its history from colonial apprenticeships and Delaware's 1783 oral quiz, through the first written exams, the NCBE's multistate tests and the Uniform Bar Exam, its format and costs, pass rates, the racial exclusion and disparities in passing, critiques of its validity, notable failures (California's glitchy exam with ChatGPT-written questions, remote exam disasters), alternatives like apprenticeships and diploma privilege, and the upcoming Next Gen bar exam. The episode closes with a listener mail about inland seas from Dylan.
topics: lawyer apprenticeship alternative to law school

segments.title: Opening banter and listener suggestion
segments.summary: The hosts joke about iHOP and Denny's, then credit listener Rowan with suggesting an episode on the bar exam.

segments.title: What the bar exam is and its purpose
segments.summary: Josh explains the bar exam as the test required to become a licensed attorney in most places, and the origin of the name from the courtroom bar railing. They note the test's purpose of protecting the public and the criticism that it goes beyond minimum competence.

segments.title: Early history: apprenticeships, first exams and Lincoln
segments.summary: Colonial lawyers apprenticed rather than attended law school. Delaware in 1783 used an informal judge quiz, and Lincoln, as a bar examiner in Illinois in the 1850s, passed a lawyer casually. The first written exam appeared in Massachusetts around 1855, law schools emerged, and the ABA favored written exams by 1921.

segments.title: Black letter law testing and the 1972 multistate test
segments.summary: In the 1930s the AALS and NCBE focused testing on black letter law. In 1972 the NCBE introduced the Multistate Bar Examination, a multiple-choice test with hypotheticals.

segments.title: Racial exclusion and early discrimination lawsuits
segments.summary: In 1912 the ABA accidentally admitted three Black attorneys, leading to a race check on applications that barred African Americans from the exam until 1943. The National Bar Association was formed in 1925. Tyler v. Vickery in Georgia challenged cut scores; the court found no intent to discriminate and held Title VII did not apply to the ABA.

segments.title: Late twentieth century changes and the Uniform Bar Exam
segments.summary: The Multistate Essay Examination was added in 1988 and the Multistate Performance Test in 1997. In 2011 most states adopted the Uniform Bar Exam combining all three tests, which made transfers between states easier but dropped state law.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Sponsor break.

segments.title: Jurisdictions, eligibility, and exam costs
segments.summary: There are 56 US jurisdictions each with its own licensing authority, usually tied to the state supreme court. Most require an ABA-accredited law school, but Washington, Virginia, Vermont, California, Maine and New York allow apprenticeship alternatives in some form. Exams are given in February and July, and registration fees, laptop fees and the bowl of tampons provided at the venue are discussed.

segments.title: Prep courses, Barbri, and the UBE format and scoring
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the cost of test prep, with Barbri holding about 60 percent market share and its origins in a merger of two companies. The UBE has MBE (200 questions, seven subjects, 50 percent), MEE (30 percent) and MPT (20 percent), spread over two days, scored on a 400-point scale with passing scores varying by state. Scores are portable for two to five years.

segments.title: Score bragging and the MPRE ethics exam
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the etiquette of sharing bar scores and the separate MPRE, a 60-question ethics test scored separately.

segments.title: Pass rates by state and internationally, retakes, and notable lawyers who failed
segments.summary: First-time pass rates in July 2025 ranged from 66 percent in Connecticut to nearly 90 percent in Utah. Some countries such as Nigeria, Singapore, Japan and Ontario are described as hard. Many successful figures failed on the first try, including Michelle Obama, Hillary Clinton, JFK Jr. and Kim Kardashian. Some jurisdictions limit retakes. Youngest passer Sophia Park passed at 17 in 2024.

segments.title: Law school accreditation and the 75 percent rule
segments.summary: The ABA requires accredited law schools to have a set share of graduates pass the bar within two years, reportedly 75 percent, or lose accreditation.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Sponsor break.

segments.title: Racial disparities in bar passage
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the diversity problem in law, citing 2021 ABA data showing white first-time takers passing at higher rates than Black, Hispanic and Native American graduates. The NCBE argues the gap reflects systemic disparities earlier in education. Critics note the burden of unpaid work during prep.

segments.title: Validity criticisms and the Nevada study
segments.summary: A 2024 Nevada study of about 500 new attorneys found bar scores minimally predictive of career success. Critics argue the NCBE has never defined legal competence, so the test may be invalid.

segments.title: Remote exam disasters and California's ChatGPT questions
segments.summary: Remote exams during COVID had crashes, facial recognition failures on dark skin, and strict eye-tracking rules. California built its own exam with software crashes and lost essays, and some questions were written by ChatGPT without review. In New York a test taker had cardiac arrest during the exam and testing continued.
topics: New York bar exam cardiac arrest

segments.title: Closed-book testing versus practice, and experienced attorneys retaking the bar
segments.summary: An Oklahoma study had successful practicing attorneys retake the bar with no prep; none passed, with scores from 26 to 52 percent. The hosts note the bar is closed-book and memorization-heavy, unlike practice.

segments.title: Alternatives: diploma privilege, apprenticeships, and the Next Gen bar
segments.summary: Wisconsin offers diploma privilege for graduates of its law schools, and New Hampshire has a similar path for honors graduates. Oregon, Vermont and Virginia allow apprenticeships in place of the bar, and Washington has a plan for 2026. California's supreme court rejected an Oregon-style apprenticeship proposal. The NCBE's Next Gen bar exam is shorter, can be taken remotely, and drops areas such as family law.

segments.title: Arguments for ending the bar and an anonymous attorney's views
segments.summary: Ending the bar could push law schools to graduate competent lawyers and lower legal fees by increasing supply. An anonymous attorney friend says the bar shows information synthesis under pressure but is weakly predictive, favors apprenticeships, and wants more emphasis on writing.

segments.title: Closing banter before listener mail
segments.summary: Brief banter about taking the bar exam for fun.

segments.title: Listener mail on inland seas
segments.summary: Listener Dylan writes about inland seas, noting that the Caspian Sea is classified as a lake, Hudson Bay is an inland sea, and the Larapentine Sea split Australia during the Cambrian.

segments.summary: Standard iHeartRadio sign-off.
